questions.q: How long did Mangalyaan’s engine really fire to brake into Mars orbit?
questions.do: In Leaving Earth one step at a time, find the Mars orbit insertion row and read the Engine time: real column.
questions.a: 1,388.67 s, about 23 minutes. The small 440-newton engine needed a long burn to remove about 1,063 m/s.

questions.q: Burn 4 on 10 November 2013 fell short. How big was its push, and how much did the unplanned extra burn the next day add?
questions.do: In the burns table, compare the Push column for Burn 4, fell short and Burn 4b, unplanned extra. Also see the first row of Checks against the real mission.
questions.a: Burn 4 gave only 35 m/s (ISRO’s figure; the model gets 32.5 m/s from the orbits). Burn 4b added about 126 m/s to finish the job and raise the far point to 118,642 km.

questions.q: Did ISRO pick good dates? Compare its trip with the cheapest pair of dates on the launch-window chart.
questions.do: In Could they have left on another day?, read the text under the chart. Then tap a few squares far from the ring and watch the total push change.
questions.a: ISRO’s dates need about 1.68 km/s in all. The cheapest pair (leave 4 Dec 2013, arrive 22 Sept 2014) needs about 1.67 km/s. So ISRO was almost exactly at the best point. Squares far from the ring need much more push.

questions.q: For the trans-Mars injection burn, the model predicts a shorter engine time than the real one. Why?
questions.do: In the burns table, compare real and predicted engine time for Trans-Mars injection. Then read What the model leaves out.
questions.a: Real 1,328.89 s, predicted about 1,219 s (−8%). The model treats every burn as instant. A real burn that lasts many minutes loses some push to gravity, so the engine had to fire longer.

questions.q: What did India achieve on 24 September 2014, and what did the mission cost?
questions.do: Read the introduction at the top of the page.
questions.a: Mangalyaan was captured by Mars after a 23-minute burn. India became the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit. It cost about ₹450 crore (US$73 million), the cheapest Mars mission to date.
